title: De Artibus Ac Disciplinis Liberalium Litterarum
author: Cassiodorus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1187.tmp1187.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Liber autem dictus est a libro, id est arboris cor- tice dempto atque liberato, ubi ante copiam charta- rum antiqui (??) describebant. Scire autem debemus sicut. Varro dicit, utilitatis alicujus causa omnium artium exstitisse principia.
passages.english: A book (liber) is so called from liber, that is, the bark of a tree stripped off and freed, on which the ancients used to write before there was a supply of paper. We ought to know, moreover, as Varro says, that the beginnings of all the arts arose for the sake of some usefulness.
passages.notes: The pun on liber (book), liber (inner bark) and liberatus (freed) is lost in English. The edition's '(??)' after 'antiqui' marks an uncertain point in the printed text. 'Chartarum' is translated as 'paper', meaning papyrus sheets. The stray full stop in 'sicut. Varro' is ignored.

passages.original: Nomina quae apud nos in us, ut vulgus, pelagus, virus, Lucretius viri dicit; quanquam rectius inflexum maneat. Secundae species sunt quae per obliquos ca- sus crescunt, et genitivo singulari in is litteras ex- eunt; ut genus, nemus : ex quibus quaedam u in e mutant, ut olus oleris, ulcus ulceris : quaedam in o, ut nemus nemoris, pecus pecoris.
passages.english: Nouns which among us [end] in -us, such as vulgus, pelagus, virus: Lucretius says viri; although it would more correctly remain uninflected. The second kind are those which increase through the oblique cases and end in the letters -is in the genitive singular, such as genus, nemus. Of these some change u into e, as olus, oleris, ulcus, ulceris; some into o, as nemus, nemoris, pecus, pecoris.
passages.notes: The opening sentence appears incomplete or abridged; the sense seems to be that such nouns are indeclinable, though Lucretius uses the genitive viri (from virus). The grammatical examples are left in Latin, since the forms themselves are the subject.

passages.original: In t littera, neutra tantum nomina quaedam, pauca finiuntur; ut git, quod non declinatur; ut caput, sin- ciput. Quidam cum lac dicunt, adjiciunt i, propter quod facit lactis; sed Virgilius :
passages.english: In the letter t only certain neuter nouns end, and few of them: such as git, which is not declined; such as caput, sinciput. Some, when they say lac, add an i [lacti], because it makes lactis; but Virgil:
passages.notes: The passage breaks off before the quotation from Virgil. The construal of 'adjiciunt i' as producing the nominative form 'lacti' is my interpretation.

passages.original: Omnis controversia, sicut ait Cicero, aut simplex est, aut juncta, aut ex comparatione.
passages.english: Every controversy, as Cicero says, is either simple, or conjoined, or [arises] from comparison.

passages.original: Convincibile est quod evidenti ratione convincitur [ms. convincit]; sicut fecit Cicero pro Milone : Ejus igitur mortis sedetis ultores, cujus vitam si pu- tetis [ed., possetis] per vos restitui posse, noletis.
passages.english: The 'convincing' [argument] is one that convinces by evident reasoning, as Cicero did in the speech for Milo: 'You sit, then, as avengers of the death of a man whose life you would refuse [to restore], if you thought it could be restored by you.'
passages.notes: Bracketed variants in the edition: ms. 'convincit' for 'convincitur'; ed. 'possetis' for 'putetis'. The translation follows the main text.

passages.original: Sententiale est quod sententia generalis addicit; ut apud Terentium : Obsequium amicos, veritas odium parit.
passages.english: The 'sentential' [argument] is one that a general maxim confirms, as in Terence: 'Compliance breeds friends, truth [breeds] hatred.'

passages.original: Exemplabile est quod alicujus exempli compara- tione eventum similem comminatur, sicut Cicero in Philippicis dicit : Te miror, Antoni, quorum facta imitere [M. G., imitaris], eorum exitus non perhor- rescere [M. G., pertimescere].
passages.english: The exemplary [argument] is that which, by comparison with some example, threatens a similar outcome, as Cicero says in the Philippics: "I am amazed, Antony, that you do not shudder at the end of those whose deeds you imitate."
passages.notes: Bracketed variants in the edition (imitaris, pertimescere) do not change the sense.

passages.original: Collectivum est, cum in unum, quae argumentata sunt, colliguntur; sicut ait Cicero pro Milone : Quem igitur cum gratia noluit, hunc voluit cum aliquorum querela, quem jure, quem loco, quem tempore non est ausus; hunc injuria, alieno tempore cum periculo capitis non dubitavit occidere.
passages.english: The 'collective' [argument] is when the points that have been argued are gathered together into one, as Cicero says in the speech for Milo: 'The man, then, whom he was unwilling [to kill] with people's goodwill, him he was willing [to kill] amid the complaints of some; the man whom he did not dare [to kill] lawfully, at a suitable place, at a suitable time, him he did not hesitate to kill unlawfully, at an unsuitable time, at the risk of his own life.'

passages.original: Nomen est vox significativa secundum placitum sine tempore : cujus nulla pars est significativa (??)- parata, ut Socrates.
passages.english: A noun is a sound that signifies by convention, without time, no part of which is significant when separated, as "Socrates".
passages.notes: The text is damaged before "-parata"; read as "separata" (separated), following Aristotle's definition.

passages.original: Enuntiativa oratio est vox significativa de eo quod est aliquid, vel non est, ut, Socrates est, Socrates non est.
passages.english: An enunciative statement is a significant utterance about whether something is or is not, as in: Socrates is, Socrates is not.
passages.notes: 'Enuntiativa oratio' is the technical term for a declarative proposition.

passages.original: Affirmatio est enuntiatio alicujus de aliquo, ut, Socrates est.
passages.english: An affirmation is the enunciation of something about something, as in: Socrates is.

passages.original: Negatio est alicujus de aliquo negatio, ut, Socrates non est.
passages.english: A negation is the denial of something about something, as in: Socrates is not.

passages.original: Contradictio est affirmationis et negationis opposi- tio, ut, Socrates disputat, Socrates non disputat.
passages.english: A contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, as in: Socrates is disputing, Socrates is not disputing.

passages.original: Nona species definitionis est quam Graeci κατά τΟποσιν, Latini per quamdam imaginationem dicunt : ut, AEneas est Veneris et Anchisae filius. Haec sem- per in individuis versatur, quae Graeci άτοαα appel- lant. Idem accidit in eo genere dictionis ubi aliquis pudor aut metus est nominare : ut Cicero, Cum me videlicet sicarii illi describant.
passages.english: The ninth kind of definition is the one the Greeks call *kata hypotyposin* and the Latins [call definition] 'by a kind of imagining', as: 'Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises.' This always deals with individuals, which the Greeks call *atoma*. The same occurs in that kind of speech where there is some shame or fear in naming [something], as Cicero: 'When, of course, those assassins describe me.'
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by scanning: 'κατά τΟποσιν' is read as κατὰ ὑποτύπωσιν, and 'άτοαα' as ἄτομα.

passages.original: Particulares vero, si quis hoc modo : quidam homo justus est, quidam homo justus non est. Indefinitae sic : homo justus est, homo justus non est. Singulares vero sunt, quae de individuo aliquid sin- gularique proponunt : ut, Cato justus est, Cato justus non est : etenim Cato individuus est ac singularis.
passages.english: Particular [propositions], if someone [speaks] in this way: 'some man is just', 'some man is not just'. Indefinite ones thus: 'man is just', 'man is not just'. Singular ones are those that propose something about an individual and single [thing], as: 'Cato is just', 'Cato is not just'; for Cato is individual and single.

passages.original: Ex transumptione vero hoc modo fit : cum ex his terminis in quibus quaestio constituta est, ad aliud quidem notius dubitatio transfertur; atque ex ejus probatione ea quae in quaestione sunt posita, confir- mantur; ut Socrates, cum quid posset in unoquoque justitia, quaereret, omnem tractatum ad reipublicae transtulit magnitudinem; atque ex eo quod illa effi- ceret in singulis, etiam valere firmavit. Qui locus a toto forsitan esse videretur;
passages.english: [Argument] from transference, however, comes about in this way: when the doubt is transferred from the terms in which the question has been set to something else that is better known, and from the proof of that, the things set out in the question are confirmed. Thus Socrates, when he was inquiring what justice could do in each individual, transferred the whole discussion to the greater scale of the state, and from what justice brought about there, he established that it also had force in individuals. This topic might perhaps seem to be [the topic] from the whole;
passages.notes: 'Transumptio' is a technical term for a dialectical topic, rendered here as 'transference'. The clause 'ex eo quod illa efficeret in singulis' literally reads 'from what it brought about in individuals'. The sense requires that what justice achieves in the state proves its force in individuals, so the reading may be corrupt or compressed.

passages.original: A toto est argumentum etiam, cum definitio adhi- betur ad id quod quaeritur; sicut ait Cicero, Gloria est laus recte factorum, magnorumque in rempubli- cam fama meritorum : ecce [ed., ex se] quia gloria lotum est, per definitionem ostendit quid sit gloria.
passages.english: There is also an argument from the whole, when a definition is applied to the thing under inquiry, as Cicero says: 'Glory is the praise of deeds rightly done and the renown of great services to the commonwealth.' See: because glory is the whole, he shows by definition what glory is.
passages.notes: 'lotum' is read as 'totum'. The edition's bracket gives the variant 'ex se' for 'ecce'.

passages.original: Primo ergo a conjugalis argumentum ducatur. Conjugata dicuntur, cum declinatur a nomine, et fit verbum; ut Cicero Verrem dicit evenisse provin- ciam; vel nomen a verbo, cum latrocinari dicitur la- tro : aut nomen a nomine; ut Terentius : Inceptio est amentium, haud amantium.
passages.english: First, then, let an argument be drawn from conjugates. Things are called conjugates when [a word] is derived from a noun and a verb is formed, as when Cicero says that the province 'happened' to Verres [evenisse, playing on Verres]; or a noun from a verb, as when a robber (latro) is said to rob (latrocinari); or a noun from a noun, as Terence: 'It is the undertaking of madmen (amentium), not of lovers (amantium).'
passages.notes: 'conjugalis' is read as 'conjugatis'. The Cicero example is obscure; it may be a wordplay on 'everrisse' (to sweep clean) and Verres, garbled here.

passages.original: A genere argumentum est, quando a re generali ad speciem aliquam descendit : ut illud Virgilii, Va- rium et mutabile semper femina : potuit et Dido, quod est species, varia ei mutabilis esse. Vel illud Ciceronis, quod fecit argumentum, descendens a ge. nere ad speciem : nam cum omnium provinciarum sociorumque rationem diligenter habere debeatis, tum praecipue Siciliae, judices.
passages.english: An argument from genus is when one descends from a general matter to some species, as in that [line] of Virgil: "A woman is always a varied and changeable thing": Dido too, who is a species, could be varied and changeable. Or that [passage] of Cicero, who made an argument descending from genus to species: "For while you ought to take careful account of all the provinces and allies, then above all of Sicily, judges."
passages.notes: "varia ei mutabilis" read as "varia et mutabilis" (scanning error).

passages.original: A specie argumentum ducitur, cum generali quae- stioni fidem species facit; ut illud Virgilii :
passages.english: An argument is drawn from species when the species lends credibility to a general question, as in that [passage] of Virgil:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: A simili argumentum est, quando de rebus ali- quibus similia proferuntur; ut Virgilius :
passages.english: An argument from the similar is when similar things are brought forward concerning certain matters, as Virgil [says]:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: A differentia argumentum ducitur, quando per differentiam aliquae res separantur; Virgilius :
passages.english: An argument is drawn from difference when certain things are separated by means of a difference; Virgil [says]:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: A contrariis argumentum sumitur, quando res dis- crepantes sibimet opponuntur; ut Terentius :
passages.english: An argument is taken from contraries when discordant things are set against one another, as Terence [says]:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: Ab antecedentibus argumentum est, quando ali- qua ex his qum prius gesta sunt comprobantur; ut Cicero pro Milone : Cum non dubitaverit aperire quid cogitaverit, vos potestis dubitare quid fecerit? Praecessit enim praedictio, ubi est argumentum, et seculum est facium.
passages.english: An argument from antecedents is when certain things are proved from those that were done earlier, as Cicero [says] in For Milo: "Since he did not hesitate to reveal what he had in mind, can you hesitate [to say] what he did?" For the prediction came first, where the argument lies, and the deed followed.
passages.notes: "qum" read as "quae", "seculum est facium" as "secutum est factum" (scanning errors).

passages.original: A repugnantibus argumentum est, quando illud quod objicitur, aliqua contrarietate destruitur; ut Cicero dicit : Is igitur non modo a te periculo libe- ratus, sed etiam honore amplissimo ditatus, argui- tur domui suae te interficere voluisse.
passages.english: An argument from incompatibles is when what is alleged is destroyed by some contradiction, as Cicero says: "This man, then, not only freed from danger by you but also enriched with the most ample honour, is accused of having wished to kill you in his own house."
passages.notes: "domui suae" taken as "domi suae" (in his own house).

passages.original: A causis argumentum est, quando ex consuetu- dine communi res quae tractatur, fieri potuisse con- vincitur; ut in Terentio :
passages.english: An argument from causes is when the matter under discussion is shown, from common custom, to have been able to happen, as in Terence:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: Ab effectibus ducitur argumentum, cum ex his quae facta sunt, aliquid approbatur; ut in Virgilio :
passages.english: An argument is drawn from effects when something is proved from the things that have been done, as in Virgil:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: A comparatione argumentum ducitur, quando per collationem personarum sive causarum, sententiae ratio confirmatur, et a majori ratione hoc modo, ut in Virgilio :
passages.english: An argument is drawn from comparison when the reasoning of a proposition is confirmed by a comparison of persons or of cases, and [it is made] from the greater in this way, as in Virgil:
passages.notes: The quotation that follows is not included in the passage.

passages.original: reliqua vero quae vel sunt adjuncta negotio, vel negotium gestum conse- quuntur, talia sunt qualia in dialecticis locis ea quae secundum Themistium quidem partim rei substan- tiam consequuntur, partim sunt extrinsecus, partim versantur in mediis; secundum Ciceronem vero in- ter affecta numerata sunt, vel extrinsecus posita.
passages.english: The remaining things, however, which are either joined to the act or follow upon the act once done, are of the same kind as those in the dialectical topics which, according to Themistius, partly follow from the substance of the thing, partly lie outside it, and partly occupy a middle position; but according to Cicero they are counted among the things affected, or [among those] placed outside.
passages.notes: "inter affecta": Cicero's category of things related or affected (adfecta) among the topics; rendering approximate.

passages.original: Nam ut Orphei lyram, Sirenarum cantus, tanquam fabulosa taceamus : quid de David dicimus, qui ab spiritu immundo Saulem disciplina saluberrimae mo- dulationis eripuit, novoque modo per auditum sani- tatem contulit regi, quam medici non poterant her- barum potestatibus operari (I Reg.XVI, 23)!
passages.english: For, to pass over in silence the lyre of Orpheus and the song of the Sirens as fabulous: what do we say of David, who by the discipline of most wholesome melody rescued Saul from the unclean spirit, and in a new way, through hearing, brought the king a health that physicians could not bring about by the powers of herbs (1 Kings 16:23)!
passages.notes: The reference "I Reg." follows the Vulgate numbering (1 Kings = 1 Samuel).

passages.original: Scripsit etiam et Pater Augustinus de musica sex libros, in quibus humanam vocem, rhythmicos sonos et harmoniam modulabilem in longis syllabis atque brevibus naturaliter habere monstravit. Censorinus quoque de accentibus voci nostrae adnecessariis subtiliter disputavit, pertinere dicens ad musicam disciplinam;
passages.english: Father Augustine also wrote six books on music, in which he showed that the human voice naturally possesses rhythmic sounds and a harmony that can be set to measure in long and short syllables. Censorinus too discussed with subtlety the accents necessary to our voice, saying that they belong to the discipline of music;
passages.notes: "adnecessariis" read as "necessariis" (possibly "ad necessariis" in the scan).
